stories.title: Goodbye Marina Square? Famous Mall to Close for a Big Makeover
stories.headline_kid: One of Singapore's well-known shopping malls, Marina Square, will close next year to be rebuilt into something much bigger.
summary: Marina Square Shopping Mall, near Marina Bay, will close its doors on 31 March 2027. It will then be torn down and rebuilt into a much bigger complex with luxury homes, a hotel, serviced apartments and offices.

This is part of a huge redevelopment plan by Singapore Land Group. The new complex is expected to be finished by 2031 - about five years from now, when today's Primary 4 pupils will be in secondary school or even older.

For decades, Marina Square has been a favourite spot for shopping, eating and watching movies, especially for families who live or work near the city. Many Singaporeans have grown up visiting the mall with their families.

This is part of a bigger trend of older buildings in Singapore being redeveloped to make better use of the land, similar to how other ageing malls across the island have been transformed over the years.

lenses.me: If you've ever visited Marina Square with your family, you'll need to say goodbye to it after March 2027 - but a shiny new complex will take its place by 2031.
lenses.family: Parents who work near Marina Bay or enjoy shopping there will need to find new places to eat, shop or catch a movie while it's being rebuilt.
lenses.friends: Your classmates who live near town might share memories of visiting Marina Square before it closes.
lenses.nation: This shows how Singapore keeps redeveloping its land to build newer, bigger complexes that combine homes, shops and offices in one place.
lenses.world: It reflects a trend seen in busy cities everywhere, where old buildings are torn down and replaced with taller, multi-use towers to fit more people and businesses.

stories.title: Long Queues Ahead: Heavy Traffic Expected at Woodlands and Tuas Checkpoints
stories.headline_kid: Planning a trip to Malaysia during the school holidays? Get ready for long queues at the checkpoints!
summary: The Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) has warned that traffic will be very heavy at the Woodlands and Tuas checkpoints from 4 to 14 September. This is because many families will be travelling to Malaysia during the September school holidays.
ICA is encouraging travellers to plan their journeys early and to try travelling during non-peak hours, such as very early morning or late at night, to avoid the worst jams.
If your family is planning a road trip to Johor Bahru or beyond, you might want to leave extra early or pack some snacks and games for the wait at the checkpoint.
This happens almost every school holiday, as many Singaporeans use the break to visit family, go shopping, or take short holidays across the Causeway or the Second Link.

lenses.me: If your family is planning a trip to Malaysia these holidays, be ready for a long wait in the car.
lenses.family: Parents planning road trips should check ICA's advice and consider leaving very early or late to skip the jam.
lenses.friends: Some of your friends might share stories about being stuck at the checkpoint for hours during the holidays.
lenses.nation: It shows how closely connected Singapore and Malaysia are, with many people crossing the border for work, school breaks and shopping.
lenses.world: Border checkpoints like these exist wherever two countries share a land border, such as between the United States and Canada.

compo_words.example: ICA issued an advisory about heavy traffic.
Traffic congestion is expected at the checkpoints.
Try to avoid travelling during peak hours.

compo_phrases.example: It's wise to plan ahead before a long journey.

stories.title: Singapore Sends Special Police Officers to Help After Nepal's Terrible Flood
stories.headline_kid: Singapore is sending trained police officers to help identify victims of the terrible Nepal flood disaster.
summary: Singapore's Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) has announced it will send police officers trained in "disaster victim identification" to Nepal. Their careful and respectful job is to help find out who each victim was, so families can finally know what happened to their loved ones.
Singapore will also send humanitarian aid, including supplies from government agencies and the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF), to help survivors who lost their homes and belongings in the disaster.

The disaster has grown even more serious. Nepal's disaster agency now says 4,247 people are missing, with 903 bodies already found. Rescuers are still digging through thick mud and debris almost a week after the flood struck.
Nepal's Prime Minister has also spoken out, saying the disaster was caused by climate change and asking the world to take the problem more seriously so tragedies like this can be prevented in future.

lenses.me: It might feel far away, but knowing that Singaporeans are helping strangers in another country shows how one small nation can make a big difference.
lenses.family: Your family might see this news and talk about why it's important to help others during disasters, even people we've never met.
lenses.friends: Your classmates might ask what "disaster victim identification" means - it's the careful work of finding out who each victim was, often using fingerprints or dental records.
lenses.nation: This shows Singapore's role as a caring neighbour in the region, always ready to send help - people, supplies or expertise - when disaster strikes.
lenses.world: It highlights how climate change is making disasters like this more frequent and severe, a problem that affects countries everywhere, not just Nepal.

compo_words.example: Experts worked hard to identify the victims of the flood.

compo_words.meaning: relating to helping people in need
compo_words.example: Singapore sent humanitarian aid to the flood victims.

compo_phrases.example: Singapore lent a helping hand to Nepal after the disaster.

stories.title: Haze Turns 'Hazardous' in Parts of Malaysia and Indonesia
stories.headline_kid: The haze has gotten so bad in parts of Malaysia and Indonesia that the air is now officially 'hazardous'.
summary: Air quality has turned "hazardous" - the worst possible level - in parts of Sarawak, Malaysia, and Indonesia's Kalimantan region on the island of Borneo. In Sarawak's Serian district, the Air Pollutant Index hit 475, while in Palangkaraya, Indonesia, the reading soared to a shocking 780.

To picture how bad this is: Singapore's own air quality index rarely goes above 100, which is already considered "unhealthy". A reading of 475 or 780 means the air is thick with smoke and can be dangerous to breathe, especially for young children, the elderly and people with breathing problems.

The haze is caused by forest and land fires in Indonesia, which happen almost every dry season when land is burned to clear it quickly and cheaply. Japan is even sending a ship to Indonesia to help fight the fires.

Singapore hasn't reported hazardous levels so far, but haze can drift across the region depending on the wind. It's worth keeping an eye on our own air quality readings and being ready to wear a mask or stay indoors if needed.

lenses.me: If you've ever noticed the sky looking grey or smelt something smoky, that's haze - and it can make it harder to play outside or do PE.
lenses.family: Families should keep N95 masks at home and check PSI (Pollutant Standards Index) readings before outdoor activities.
lenses.friends: If your friends live in Malaysia or Indonesia, they might be affected much more seriously - some schools there may even close because of the smoke.
lenses.nation: Singapore has faced haze from Indonesia's fires for decades and has systems like PSI readings and public advisories to help residents stay safe.
lenses.world: This shows how one country's environmental problem, like forest fires, can affect the health and daily lives of people in neighbouring countries.

compo_words.example: The air quality reached hazardous levels this week.

stories.title: Singapore's Veteran Diplomat Tommy Koh Wins Asia's Top Award
stories.headline_kid: Singapore's veteran diplomat Professor Tommy Koh, 88, has just won one of Asia's most prestigious awards!
summary: Professor Tommy Koh, a well-known Singaporean diplomat and lawyer, has won the Ramon Magsaysay Award. This award is often called "Asia's Nobel Prize" because it honours people who have done outstanding work for their communities or the world.

Prof Koh, who is 88 years old, was recognised for his decades of work in international diplomacy. He has helped countries talk through their disagreements peacefully instead of fighting, and represented Singapore in important discussions around the world, including talks on the law of the sea.
He is one of three people from across Asia to receive the award this year. The award foundation praised him as an "exemplary leader" who has spent his life encouraging dialogue between nations.
This is a proud moment for Singapore. It shows that even a small country can produce world-class diplomats who help solve big problems between nations.

lenses.me: Prof Koh shows that being a good listener and communicator can help solve even the biggest disagreements - a skill useful even in your own friendships.
lenses.family: Your family might be proud that a fellow Singaporean has been honoured on such an international stage.
lenses.friends: You and your friends could discuss what it means to be a "diplomat" and why talking things out is often better than fighting.
lenses.nation: This award brings honour to Singapore and shows the important role our small country has played in world affairs.
lenses.world: It highlights the value of peaceful dialogue between nations, especially in a world where conflicts often make the headlines.

compo_words.meaning: a person who represents their country and handles relations with other countries
